title: Visual and acoustic discomfort: A comparative study of impacts on individuals with and without ADHD using electroencephalogram (EEG)
research_question: How do specific lighting and sound conditions impact individuals with and without Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) in terms of comfort perception, task performance, eye pupil diameter, heart rate, skin temperature, and brain activity (EEG)?

participants.description: 10 males, 17 females, aged between 18 and 34 years (mean = 26.3, SD = 4.37). 14 participants were diagnosed with ADHD and continued their medication regimen; 13 reported no ADHD diagnosis. All had normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
participants.recruitment: Recruited for this experiment (details not specified beyond this statement).

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Six controlled laboratory environmental conditions with modified lighting and sound designs. Lighting conditions included: (1) Warm light (3500 K, 350 lx), (2) Cool light (6500 K, 830 lx), (3) Flickering light (3500 K, 5-10 Hz, 50-830 lx random brightness). Sound conditions included: (1) Silence, (2) White noise (40 dB), (3) Classroom noise (75 dB). Conditions were permutations: Warm-Silent, Cool-Silent, Warm-White, Warm-Noisy, Cool-Noisy, Flicker-Silent.

mechanisms: Non-ADHD brains amplify information segregation mechanisms as a self-tuning response to counteract environmental discomfort, involving elevated alpha activity and decreased theta to suppress distractions and maintain focus.

Brain criticality: Neural networks self-organize into a critical state to activate optimal computational and processing characteristics (e.g., enhanced information transmission and storage) when experiencing environmental discomfort.

Lack of adaptive mechanism in ADHD individuals: ADHD participants do not exhibit the same neuro-response to discomfort, suggesting a lack of (or delay in) a certain autonomic response or capability to enhance brain functions when facing environmental discomfort.
implementation_implications: Design adaptive spaces that cater to a broad spectrum of sensory experiences, recognizing and accommodating diverse sensory responses of individuals.
Create truly neuro-inclusive built environments by tailoring spaces to the nuanced needs and preferences of neurodivergent individuals.
Proactively reduce environmental factors that may induce sensory overload or increased stress.

EEG can be used as an early detection tool for environmental discomfort, potentially informing Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCI) systems to automatically adjust environmental settings (e.g., lighting, temperature) based on individual brain responses.

limitations: Limited number of participants and demographic diversity (age ranges, cultural backgrounds).
Lack of qualitative feedback (open-ended surveys or semi-structured interviews).
Absence of peak wavelength measurement for light, limiting analysis of non-visual effects.
EEG cap itself may introduce discomfort, potentially influencing results.
EEG is highly sensitive to movement, requiring participants to minimize abrupt movements.
Real-world deployment of EEG is currently time-consuming, costly, and requires expertise.
The study is preliminary and has a limited set of conditions, requiring replication with similar and other neurodivergent populations (e.g., autism, dyslexia).
Other dimensions of environmental comfort (e.g., thermal, air quality) were not examined.
